name: Biotin
lead: Biotin, also called vitamin B7 or vitamin H, is a water-soluble B vitamin that serves as a cofactor for five human carboxylase enzymes involved in fatty acid, glucose and amino acid metabolism [1][2]. It is found in foods such as organ meats and egg yolks, and is sold as a dietary supplement alone or in multivitamins, commonly in doses of 1 to 10 mg marketed for hair and nail health [1].

Biotin deficiency is described as rare, and it can cause hair thinning, brittle nails and a facial skin rash [1]. Reviews of biotin for hair report that evidence in people with normal biotin status is limited: a 2017 review found 18 case reports of benefit, all in people with an underlying cause, and a 2024 review found three eligible studies, with the highest-quality placebo-controlled trial showing no difference from placebo [3][4].

Regulators and laboratory researchers have also documented that high-dose biotin can interfere with blood tests that use biotin-streptavidin technology, including thyroid and other hormone assays, producing falsely high or low results [1][5][6].
infobox: None set; adverse effects of high intake not determined [1]

paras: Biotin is required for normal metabolism, and supplementation is the treatment for biotinidase deficiency and other genetic disorders of biotin handling, which can be fatal if untreated [1]. Newborn screening for biotinidase deficiency began in the United States in 1984 [1]. Large-dose biotin has been studied as a therapy for multiple sclerosis, and Wikipedia mentions 300 mg per day in that context [1][8].

Biotin is widely taken for hair, skin and nail quality, a use supported by its role in keratin-related metabolism and by the hair thinning seen in deficiency [1][4]. One randomised crossover trial in men compared 5% topical minoxidil, 5 mg oral biotin and the combination [9].

A 2017 systematic review of case reports and randomised trials found 18 reported cases of biotin use for hair or nail changes; all patients had an underlying pathology, such as uncombable hair syndrome or brittle nails, and all improved. The authors concluded that evidence for use in healthy people is limited [3].

A 2024 review of oral biotin for hair growth or quality, excluding case reports, identified three studies. The highest quality was double-blind and placebo-controlled and found no difference in hair growth between biotin and placebo. The other two studied people on isotretinoin and women after sleeve gastrectomy, had potential biases, and showed no striking benefit [4].

A 2024 randomised crossover trial in men compared 5% topical minoxidil, 5 mg oral biotin and both together over hair growth outcomes [9]. The dossier lists the report as a letter, and its detailed results are not reproduced here.

Studies of biotin interference with laboratory tests include a 2017 JAMA study of healthy adults [6], a 2022 study of serum biotin interference in hormone immunoassays [10], and registered studies of biotin supplementation and routine laboratory values [11][12].

No upper intake limit has been set in the United States or by the European Food Safety Authority because adverse effects of high biotin intake have not been determined [1]. Absorption of supplemental biotin is described as non-saturable, with excess excreted in urine [1].

The principal documented concern is analytical. Intake of 5 mg per day or more can raise plasma levels enough to interfere unpredictably with biotin-streptavidin immunoassays used to measure thyroid hormones, vitamin D and other analytes [1]. A review noted potentially dangerous erroneous results in people consuming large amounts [13]. The JAMA 2017 study examined assay performance after biotin ingestion in healthy adults [6].

Biotin is attached by holocarboxylase synthetase to acetyl-CoA carboxylases 1 and 2, pyruvate carboxylase, methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase and propionyl-CoA carboxylase. It is also attached to histones, affecting chromatin structure and gene regulation [1][14]. Intestinal bacteria synthesise biotin, and dietary biotin is freed from protein by biotinidase [1].

Factors linked to higher requirement or lower levels include chronic alcohol use, some anticonvulsants, partial gastrectomy, and pregnancy and lactation; marginal deficiency has been reported in human pregnancy [1][13]. Raw egg whites contain avidin, which binds biotin, according to Grokipedia [7].

US labeling reference values were revised in 2016 from 300 to 30 micrograms per day, with compliance required in 2020 to 2021 [1]. A review of the micronutrient literature is available from ESPEN [15]. Biotin is also used widely in biotechnology as a labelling and purification tag [1][16].
